quality.conclusion:
Explanation. The laboratory behaves as a memoryless, saturating read-out of the current input multiplied by a single monotonically depleting internal resource: y[t] = g(u[t]) * S[t], with S[t] = exp(-k * sum_{s<t} h(u[s])), h(u) approximately proportional to u, and g(u) a saturating (Hill/Michaelis-Menten-like) gain with g(0)=0. Hand fits over the 19 acquired protocols give A~2.26, K~0.39, k~0.082 per unit cumulative input; the submitted predictor refits A, K, Hill exponent n, k and consumption exponent m robustly to all observations rather than hardcoding these numbers.

Tested support. (1) No dynamics in the read-out: in idea-4e8b3f trial 1 the output falls from 0.939 to -0.019 in one second when u goes 1 -> 0 and rises back to 0.853 when u returns to 1, so the fast response is an input gate, not a relaxation. (2) The hidden state is a function of cumulative input, not of path or elapsed time: at cumulative input ~10 three very different histories (sustained u=0.25, 50% duty cycling, and u=1 pulses separated by long idle periods) read u=1 gains of 0.731, 0.726 and 0.749; and in idea-4e8b3f, 40 idle seconds after cumulative 8 gave 0.8625 at a u=1 probe versus 0.8530 after only 2 idle seconds (difference 0.0095, below the 0.015 noise sigma), so idle time neither depletes nor regenerates measurably. (3) Consumption scales with u: sustained per-second log-decay is 0.0824, 0.0410, 0.0208 at u=1, 0.5, 0.25 (~4:2:1). (4) The gain is strongly sublinear: initial y is 1.632 at u=1, 1.300 at u=0.5, 0.909 at u=0.25, 0.466 at u=0.1 - far above the linear prediction at small u, which rules out the frozen reference model (exponential decline with cumulative input scaled linearly by current input) and explains why an input-proportional gain underestimates small-u responses. (5) Forward check on data not used to build the hypothesis: the model predicted 1.181 and 0.680 for the u=1 and u=0.3 probe pulses following 40 s at u=0.1 in idea-4e8b3f trial 3; measured values were 1.1819 and 0.6806. Long runs also approach zero (u=1 for 80 s ends at 0.017, within noise of 0), consistent with exhaustible, non-renewing capacity.

Remaining uncertainty. The exact shape of g at low input is not pinned down: a pure Michaelis-Menten form under-predicts the u=0.1 initial reading by about 2 sigma while over-predicting u=0.5 and u=0.25 by a similar amount, so a Hill exponent slightly above 1 or a different saturating family may be needed; the predictor leaves n free. Whether h(u) is exactly linear in u is likewise only established at u in {0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0}; a mild exponent m is left free. Estimated k varies between about 0.072 and 0.083 across subsets (idea-f2f66d late sweep versus idea-675f71 matched-cumulative probes), a 2-3 sigma spread that could indicate a small second-order effect such as slight regeneration at very low state, weak input-dependence of the consumption efficiency, or simply correlated noise. No experiment probed inputs between 0.5 and 1.0 or very small non-zero inputs below 0.1, so extrapolation there rests on the fitted smooth form. A useful predictive fit is not proof of mechanism: any held-out sequence showing gain recovery after rest, a lag after an input step, or decay departing from the cumulative-input law would falsify this single-resource account and argue for a hidden second state.

Explanation. All 19 acquired protocols are well described by a separable input-output law y[t] = S[t] * f(u[t]) where f is an instantaneous saturating readout of the current input and S is a single hidden scalar 'availability' state that is depleted by input and recovers when input is low: dS/dt = -d0*u^p*S + r0*(1-u)^q*(1-S), with S at fresh preparation near 1. The submitted predictor refits A, K, n, d0, r0, p, q, S0 to the full dataset by weighted least squares (sigma = 0.015); the state equation is linear in S for piecewise-constant u, so each one-second interval is advanced exactly.

Tested support. (1) Instantaneous readout, continuous state: at a step change the first post-switch sample jumps by the ratio of f values with S unchanged. In idea-5a6137 trial 3 the u=0.3 plateau y=0.820 is followed immediately by y=1.265 at u=0.9 (ratio 1.543), matching f(0.9)/f(0.3)=1.549 from the independent low-u pulse ladder of idea-61b36d (A~2.12, K~0.34), which itself reproduced f(0.05)=0.271 vs 0.267, f(0.2)=0.777 vs 0.783, f(0.6)=1.352 vs 1.354. (2) f(0)=0 and the state is unobservable at u=0: in idea-5a6137 trial 1 every u=0 sample scatters about zero with spread comparable to sigma even when the interleaved u=0.3 probes show the state has recovered to ~0.97. (3) Reversibility and its rate: the 0.3/0 pulse train in idea-5a6137 trial 1 recovers from S~0.089 (y=0.089 at t=30 after 30 s at u=1) back toward full availability, and the single-state law predicts y=0.483 and 0.700 at t=34 and t=38 versus measured 0.465 and 0.693. Hence the depletion caused by a long u=1 exposure is essentially fully reversible; there is no evidence for a large irreversible component on these timescales. (4) Steady states depend on u as predicted: the u=0.3 plateau y~0.82 gives S_eq~0.825 versus the model's r0(1-u)/(d0*u+r0(1-u))~0.81, and long u=1 runs decay quasi-exponentially toward zero (idea-e24cc6: y=0.043 at t=47), i.e. S_eq(u=1)=0. (5) Law of depletion: idea-61b36d's plateau ladder discriminated depletion linear in u (measured plateaus ~0.70 at u=0.2 and ~0.77 at u=0.6) from flux/saturation-driven depletion, which predicted ~0.59 and ~0.64 and is therefore disfavoured.

Remaining uncertainty. The main untested structural claim is that ONE relaxation time suffices. The clearest tension is the u=0.9 window of idea-5a6137 trial 3, which decayed to y=0.475 while the single-state fit predicts ~0.433 (about 2-3 sigma); a second slower state, a weakly nonlinear depletion order, or a mild state dependence of the readout would all produce this signature, and my experiments cannot separate them. Also untested: whether the readout is exactly hyperbolic rather than another saturating shape (only four input levels were calibrated in the ladder), whether S can exceed its fresh value (no overshoot was observed), and behaviour at rapid sub-second switching, which the protocol cannot probe. I therefore present this as a validated predictive representation of the system's response, not as an identified physical mechanism; a good RMSE on the held-out sequences would support the separable one-state description, and a large error on long high-u or fast-switching sequences would be the expected counterexample pointing to multi-timescale state dynamics.

Explanation: the measured output is the product of an instantaneous, saturating gain of the current input, g(u) (g(0)=0, roughly Michaelis-Menten with gmax~2.24, K~0.37, so g(1)~1.63, g(0.5)~1.29, g(0.15)~0.65, g(0.05)~0.25), and a hidden depletable state x that starts at 1 in every fresh preparation and is consumed only while input is applied, approximately dx/dt=-k*u*x with k~0.082/s (x depends on cumulative input, not elapsed time). Tested support: (1) g(0)=0 exactly within noise at u=0 in idea-1a8ed6 and idea-1f3647; (2) no recovery during 20 s rest (idea-1a8ed6: 1.100 observed vs 1.085 predicted on return to u=1) and equal cumulative-input protocols giving equal outputs (0.25->1 vs continuous, 1.103 vs 1.100); (3) decay at u=1 is exponential over 80 s (1.629->0.017, rate 0.080/s) and rates at u=0.25 (0.0204) and u=0.15 over 40 s (0.0125) scale linearly with u; (4) ramp protocol peaks in idea-1f3647 (1.129, 0.517, 0.328 at cumulative u 4.5, 14.5, 20) match exp(-0.082*cumulative u) times g(1) within 0.02. Alternative in which consumption is driven by the output rather than the input is rejected (it predicts 0.032/s at u=0.15, observed 0.0125). Remaining uncertainty: consumption at very low input (u=0.05 hold decayed at ~0.0025/s vs 0.0041 predicted; subsequent u=1 step 1.304 vs 1.278) hints at slightly sub-linear consumption below u~0.15, so the frozen predictor fits a consumption exponent p and a Hill exponent n rather than fixing them; the exact functional form of g between sampled levels, any small floor in x at very large cumulative input, and behaviour under inputs changing faster than 1 s are not established. A low prediction error would support this representation as useful, not prove the underlying mechanism.

Explanation: the measured output is the product of an instantaneous, saturating gain on the current input, f(u) (f(0)=0, f(1)~1.63, Hill-like with half-saturation near u~0.36), and a hidden capacity S that starts at 1, is depleted in proportion to the applied input (rate ~0.083 per second at u=1) and recovers toward 1 in proportion to the unused input (rate ~0.13-0.15 per second at u=0). Tested support: single-exponential decay under constant u=1 down to S~0.03 over 45 s; y~0 whenever u=0 regardless of history; recovery after 5-30 s rest returns S toward but never above the fresh level; an intermediate hold at u=0.5 after deep depletion relaxes upward to S~0.6, consistent with the steady state r/(k+r); alternating 1/0, 1/0.5 and 0.8/0.2 sequences are reproduced to about twice the 0.015 noise by the same bookkeeping. The frozen reference (cumulative-input decay without recovery) cannot produce the observed rises during partial input or after rest. Remaining uncertainty: recovery after short rests appears slightly faster (~5%) than the fitted one-state model predicts, which could indicate a small second timescale or a different low-u gain shape; the exact functional forms of f(u) and of the u-dependence of depletion and recovery are chosen for fit, not derived; a single-state multiplicative model that predicts well is not proof of the underlying mechanism.

question: Can a model choose interventions, test competing explanations, revise its representation and predict unseen input sequences, beyond fixed-candidate tuning?
scope: Two synthetic worlds with identical initial observations; normal model calls choose input sequences and freely authored code. The model knows general task rules and the simple reference, not the simulator equations or confirmation outputs. This is a constrained scientific-reasoning exercise, not novel real-world science.
